paragraphs.text: Vertical farming grows crops in stacked layers inside buildings, using artificial light and controlled temperature. Because plants are grown indoors, farmers need no soil; instead, roots are supplied with water containing nutrients, a method known as hydroponics.

Supporters claim that vertical farms use up to 95 percent less water than traditional fields and can be built in cities, close to customers. This reduces the distance food must travel. Critics, however, point out that the electricity needed for lighting makes the process expensive, and so far most farms grow only leafy vegetables and herbs rather than staple crops such as wheat or rice.

paragraphs.text: Octopuses are among the most intelligent invertebrates. In laboratory tests they have learned to open jars, solve mazes and recognise individual human keepers. Their intelligence is partly explained by their nervous system: roughly two thirds of their neurons are located in their arms rather than in the brain.

Despite this, octopuses are short-lived. Most species live for only one to two years, and females die soon after their eggs hatch. Scientists believe this short lifespan limits the amount of knowledge that can be passed between generations.

paragraphs.text: It is often said that children learn languages more easily than adults, and many parents rush to enrol toddlers in language classes. Yet research suggests this belief is only partly true. Adults generally learn grammar rules faster than children, and they can use study strategies that young learners cannot.

The real advantage of children is pronunciation: those who begin before puberty are far more likely to speak without a foreign accent. In my view, though, accent matters much less than being understood, and adults should not be discouraged from starting. A confident adult learner can reach a high level of fluency within a few years.

paragraphs.text: Noise in cities has risen steadily over the past fifty years. Traffic is the largest source, followed by construction and aircraft, and measurements show that some streets now exceed the levels recommended by health authorities.

Long exposure to loud sound is linked to sleep disturbance and raised blood pressure. A study of residents living near an airport found that children there scored lower in reading tests than those in quieter areas.
Some cities have responded with practical measures. Amsterdam has introduced quieter road surfaces, while Paris restricts the hours when delivery lorries may operate in residential districts.
Architects can also help. Buildings with thick glazing and courtyards facing away from main roads can reduce indoor noise dramatically, and trees planted along streets have a small but useful effect.
Not all noise is unwelcome, however. Researchers have found that the sounds of running water and birdsong lower stress, and some planners now design parks to make these sounds more noticeable.

passage.title: The Hidden Costs of Cheap Clothing

paragraphs.text: Fast fashion brands now release new collections every few weeks, encouraging shoppers to buy far more clothes than they need. The average consumer today buys around sixty percent more garments than in the year 2000, but keeps each item for half as long.

Producing cotton demands huge amounts of water; a single T-shirt can require over two thousand litres. In regions where cotton is farmed intensively, rivers and lakes have shrunk and local farmers struggle to irrigate their own crops.

Most garments are sewn in factories in countries where wages are low. Investigations have revealed long working hours and unsafe buildings, and a number of well-known brands have faced public pressure to improve conditions.
When clothes are thrown away, most end up in landfill, where synthetic fibres can take hundreds of years to break down. Only a small fraction of discarded textiles are recycled into new products.

Some companies are now trying a different approach, offering repair services, rental schemes and clothing made from recycled fibres. Whether such ideas can change the habits of shoppers remains to be seen.

paragraphs.text: Otto Lilienthal, a German engineer, made more than two thousand flights in gliders during the 1890s. He published detailed measurements of wing shapes, which later inventors relied on. He died in 1896 when one of his gliders stalled and crashed.

Wilbur and Orville Wright, bicycle makers from Ohio, studied Lilienthal's data but found errors in it. They built their own wind tunnel to test wing designs and, in 1903, made the first controlled, powered flight of a heavier-than-air machine.

Alberto Santos-Dumont, a Brazilian living in Paris, first became famous for flying small airships around the Eiffel Tower. In 1906 he flew a powered aeroplane in public in front of a large crowd, and he later gave away his designs freely so that others could build them.

paragraphs.text: Large volcanic eruptions can change the climate for several years. When a volcano erupts violently, it throws sulphur dioxide high into the atmosphere, where it forms tiny droplets that reflect sunlight back into space. As a result, the surface of the Earth cools.

The eruption of Mount Pinatubo in 1991 lowered global temperatures by about half a degree Celsius for roughly two years. In contrast, the eruption of Tambora in 1815 led to the 'year without a summer' in 1816, when crop failures caused hunger across Europe and North America.

Eruptions also release carbon dioxide, but in amounts far smaller than those produced by human activity. Scientists therefore regard volcanoes as a short-term influence on climate rather than a cause of long-term warming.

paragraphs.text: Honeybees communicate the location of food through a movement called the waggle dance. The dancing bee moves in a figure of eight, and the angle of her central run shows the direction of the food relative to the sun. The longer the dance lasts, the farther away the food is.

Other bees follow the dancer closely in the dark hive, touching her with their antennae. Scientists first decoded this system in the 1940s, and the discoverer, Karl von Frisch, later won a Nobel Prize for his work.

paragraphs.text: Before the mid-fifteenth century, books in Europe were copied by hand, mostly by monks, and a single volume could take months to finish. Johannes Gutenberg changed this around 1450 by developing a press that used movable metal type. Individual letters could be arranged into pages, inked, and pressed onto paper, then rearranged for the next page.

As books became cheaper, literacy rose quickly. By 1500, printing presses in more than two hundred European cities had produced millions of books. Ideas spread faster than ever before, and the Protestant Reformation of the sixteenth century owed much to printed pamphlets.

paragraphs.text: Solar panels convert sunlight directly into electricity, and their cost has fallen by about ninety percent in the past decade. They work best in sunny regions, but their output drops at night.

Wind turbines, in contrast, can generate power day and night, though they need steady wind and are often built at sea, where wind is stronger. Hydropower, the oldest of the three, uses falling water to turn turbines. It provides reliable energy, but large dams can force people from their homes and damage river ecosystems.

paragraphs.text: Recycling paper begins with collection. Used paper is gathered from homes and offices and taken to a recycling plant, where it is sorted by quality. The paper is then mixed with water and chemicals and broken down into a soft pulp.

Next, the pulp passes through screens that remove staples, plastic and other waste. Ink is then removed by blowing air through the mixture, which makes the ink float to the surface. Finally, the cleaned pulp is pressed flat, dried and rolled into new sheets.

paragraphs.text: Giant pandas live in the mountain forests of central China. Although they belong to the order of carnivores, around ninety-nine percent of their diet is bamboo, and an adult may eat up to fourteen kilograms a day. Because bamboo provides little energy, pandas spend most of their day eating and resting.

Pandas were once classed as endangered, but conservation work, including the creation of protected reserves and bamboo corridors linking forests, has helped numbers recover. In 2016 the species was reclassified as vulnerable, and about 1,800 wild pandas are now thought to exist.
